title: Lessons from creating the UK’s first “super-university” group
summary: Jane Harrington, Georgina Randsley de Moura, and Mark Preston set out what a year of merger-building taught them about trust, governance and communicating through uncertainty
full_text:
The challenges facing our sector are well documented.

Universities have been navigating years of financial pressure, changing student expectations, increasing regulatory complexity, geopolitical uncertainty and growing demands to demonstrate impact for students, employers and communities.

Against this backdrop, it would have been easy to focus solely on short-term pressures.

Instead, we chose to focus on the long term.

Today, as we officially launch the London and South East University Group (LASE) – bringing together the University of Greenwich and the University of Kent as the UK’s first multi-university group – we can reflect on what we have learned over the last year.

Together, our institutions span South East London, Medway and Kent, serving diverse communities with different opportunities and challenges. By combining our strengths through a new university group model, we can create a stronger platform to widen access to higher education, address skills shortages, support economic growth and increase the impact of our teaching and research across the wider region.

Equally importantly, we can create greater opportunities for our students. From day one, students across the group have access to four campuses, additional facilities, libraries and can request access to support services at a location that works best for them. Over time, our scale will enable us to strengthen partnerships with employers, expand opportunities for collaboration, and deliver an even richer student experience.

We can also build greater capacity in areas where our institutions share common strengths and ambitions. Whether supporting health and wellbeing, driving innovation in food and sustainability, strengthening the creative industries or helping tackle wider societal challenges, we believe we can achieve more for our communities by working together than we could alone.

In short, LASE was created to respond to the challenges facing higher education as well as to make a bigger difference to the students, communities and region we exist to serve.

Our approach may not work for everyone, but it does create a model for universities considering a group structure, and we want to share our learnings to benefit others.

Do it for the right reasons

Perhaps the most important lesson is that collaboration should be driven by opportunity, not simply by necessity.

Much discussion about HE mergers starts from a position of difficulty. While sector challenges are real, a merger is not a solution to unresolved institutional problems.

From the outset, our conversations were centred on potential, not survival. We believed there was an opportunity to create something greater than the sum of its parts.

No amount of financial modelling, legal agreements or organisational design can compensate for a lack of trust between institutions. Long before formal due diligence began, significant effort was invested in building relationships, understanding each other’s perspectives and establishing shared principles and values.

For institutions considering collaboration, our advice is simple: start with purpose, build relationships and be honest about what you are trying to achieve.

Trust is fundamental and the fact that both vice-chancellors worked together and were always willing to have the difficult conversation made it far easier to achieve.

Governance can be a catalyst for transformation

Large-scale institutional change requires more than executive commitment. It requires governors willing to engage deeply with complexity, ask difficult questions, and provide confidence and challenge in equal measure.

Governing bodies at both institutions invested significant time in understanding the opportunities and risks associated with creating a new university group, while remaining focused on their responsibilities to students, staff and the long-term sustainability of their institutions.

Governance structures must be both robust and adaptable. Traditional governance arrangements are not always designed with innovative collaborative models in mind.

For institutions considering similar approaches, our advice would be to engage governing bodies early and meaningfully. Transformational change cannot be delegated to a small project team. Governors and executive leaders must develop a shared understanding of the vision, the challenges and the outcomes they are seeking to achieve. When that alignment exists, governance becomes a powerful source of momentum rather than merely a mechanism for oversight.

Communications and engagement are leadership responsibilities

One of the greatest temptations during a complex transformation is to wait until every detail is confirmed before communicating. In reality, staff and students often need communication most when there is uncertainty. Silence can quickly be filled by speculation, assumptions and misinformation.

Communications have been at the heart of the programme since the start.

We have prioritised regular engagement with staff, students, governors and external stakeholders. Engagement began well before the merger completed. We brought together executive leadership teams from both institutions, and extended those conversations to wider teams. We also delivered 18 engagement sessions over a three-month period across our four campus locations to more than 1,000 staff.

We also worked hard to create multiple opportunities for colleagues to engage with the process, ask questions and share feedback. Our all-staff sessions were complemented by regular written communications and direct engagement from us.

Visible leadership proved particularly important. People understandably look to leaders for direction during periods of change, and there is no substitute for being present, accessible and willing to engage with difficult questions. While we could not always provide immediate answers, we could explain what we knew, what we were still working through and how decisions would be made.

Engagement was never intended to be a one-way process. There have been occasions when colleagues challenged our assumptions, highlighted unintended consequences or told us that aspects of our approach were not landing in the way we had intended. Creating the space for honest feedback helped us refine our plans, improve our communications and better understand the concerns and priorities of different groups across our institutions.

That approach helped us navigate a period that inevitably contained ambiguity while maintaining confidence in the direction of travel. Most importantly, it reinforced a principle that will continue to guide LASE in the years ahead: people are more likely to support change when they feel informed, involved, listened to and part of shaping the future.

The legal completion of our merger on 1 August and the official launch of LASE are significant milestones. They represent the culmination of an extraordinary amount of work by staff, governors and partners. But they are milestones, not endpoints. The real measure of success will be what we deliver in the years ahead.

Higher education has a proud history of innovation. The challenges facing the sector today require that spirit of innovation more than ever. Collaboration will not be the answer for every institution, but we believe it should be part of the conversation.

Over the coming months, we will begin work on a blueprint for the sector, sharing in greater detail the lessons, challenges and insights from this first chapter of the LASE story.

As the first institutions to create a university group of this kind in the UK, we believe there is a responsibility to share openly not only what worked, but also the complexities we encountered along the way. We hope this blueprint will provide practical guidance for institutions exploring their own collaborative futures and contribute to a wider conversation about how higher education can innovate, adapt and thrive in the years ahead.

The post Rigour and warmth are not a trade-off: academic conduct needs less policing and more care appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
Join the Policy Institute at King’s College London and HEPI on Tuesday 15 September, from 6.30pm to 7.45pm, at Bush House, London, for a free event exploring the future of higher education in England. Drawing on Professor Sir Chris Husbands’ report, New choices: Revisiting futures for higher education in England, the discussion will consider how financial pressures, generative AI, changing student expectations and declining public trust are reshaping the sector – and the choices universities and government need to make now to secure a sustainable future. Register here.

This blog was kindly authored by Dr Chelle Oldham, The Open University & University of Glasgow, University Academic Integrity Co-Lead.

Generative AI has done something to academic conduct that no policy review ever managed: it has made the caseload impossible to ignore – referrals are up across the sector and detection tools are flagging work at volume. The institutional reflex under that pressure, understandable but wrong, is to police harder. Tighten the rules, catch more, move faster. I want to suggest the opposite. The conduct conversation is one of the few moments where a university decides, in practice, what kind of institution it is, and the evidence of my own caseload is that we get fairer, more defensible and more honest outcomes when we lead with compassion rather than suspicion.

Compassion here is not the soft option, and it is emphatically not about lowering standards. It means holding students to high standards while assuming good faith and giving them the support to meet them. Rigour without warmth produces a process that is correct and unjust at the same time; warmth without rigour helps no one. The skill (and it is a skill, not a personality trait) is holding both. In practice, that starts with curiosity rather than accusation: when something looks wrong, the most useful opening is a question, not a verdict. Most of what surfaces turns out to be a gap in learning, not dishonesty: often a student leaning on assistive tools they were entitled to use, who never knew where the line sat.

This matters more sharply in the AI era because of who gets flagged. Detection tools do not catch dishonesty; they catch difference. The students most likely to be marked out by an unusual style or a probability score are disproportionately neurodivergent, disabled, or writing in English as an additional language. In 2026, we are investigating students for using text-to-speech software, spelling tools and AI-assisted writing aids that were, in many cases, recommended to them through their Disabled Students’ Allowance. We are, in effect, policing the very accommodations we prescribed. A growing body of research confirms far higher false-positive rates for exactly these students, penalising those who are not cheating on suspicion alone. A flag is a reason to ask a question. It is never, on its own, a conclusion. Treating it as proof does not just risk an individual injustice; it builds a process that systematically disadvantages the very students our equality duties exist to protect. As Sarah Eaton puts it, ‘there can be no integrity without equity’.

Conduct work can also land at one of the hardest moments in a student’s life, when the allegation is the least of what someone is carrying. The line I hold onto is that a conduct officer is not a clinician and does not need to be. The role is to run a fair process with care and to connect the student to people who can help, not to diagnose or counsel. That clarity is liberating. It means signposting wellbeing support early, making the process itself accessible, and being willing to pause when a student is too unwell to engage fairly. You can take an alleged breach seriously and treat the person with care at the same time; these are not in tension.

The sector now has a hard reason to take this seriously as well as a moral one. The Abrahart litigation has made plain that a university’s duty of care and its anticipatory equality duties are not aspirational language in a strategy document. They are enforceable, and they apply to the processes we run as much as to the teaching we deliver. A conduct process designed only for the confident, well and articulate student is not a defensible process. It is a liability that happens to look like rigour.

The constructive alternative is not more surveillance but better education, delivered earlier. The Educate–Enable–Expect model I have argued for elsewhere starts from the premise that most students want to do the right thing and that our job is to make sure they know how: educate them about what integrity means in practice, including how their assistive tools interact with assessment; enable them to practise in formative spaces before the high-stakes moment; and only then expect them to take ownership. For disabled students navigating already-complex accommodation landscapes, that sequence is not just pedagogically sound: it is the fair one.

None of this requires new policy. It requires us to stop treating compassion and rigour as a trade-off and to build the alternative into how we train and support conduct officers from the start. Difference is not dishonesty. A flag is not a finding. And a fair process, run with care, is the most rigorous one we have.

title: ‘Gigantic spaceship’: University of Bristol’s flagship £500m campus opens
summary:
Temple Quarter Enterprise Campus near to station will make it easier for students and staff to commute

Not so long ago, the first impression for visitors arriving by train to Bristol’s main railway station was a derelict building described by David Cameron as looking like the entrance to a war zone.

On Monday, a shiny new University of Bristol campus on the site of that crumbling Royal Mail sorting office next door to Temple Meads is opening its doors to students, teachers and members of the public.

full_text:
Not so long ago, the first impression for visitors arriving by train to Bristol’s main railway station was a derelict building described by David Cameron as looking like the entrance to a war zone.

On Monday, a shiny new University of Bristol campus on the site of that crumbling Royal Mail sorting office next door to Temple Meads is opening its doors to students, teachers and members of the public.

The proximity of the Temple Quarter Enterprise Campus (TQEC) to the station should make it easier for students and staff who cannot afford Bristol’s expensive property and rental market to commute, and for business and research partners from all across the country to attend meetings.

The campus is also designed to be “porous”, with many areas completely open to the public, turning it into a front door to the university for Bristolians in a way that its grand buildings high on the hill in the leafy Clifton area never have been.

The £500m campus is a major part of one of the UK’s biggest regeneration schemes, Bristol Temple Quarter, which is to bring thousands of new homes, work spaces and health and education centres to one of the city’s – and England’s – most deprived neighbourhoods. The scheme is so important to Labour locally and nationally that it got a mention in Andy Burnham’s first prime minister’s questions.

Speaking in a garden space in TQEC almost directly above Temple Meads’ platform 15, Judith Squires, deputy vice chancellor and university lead for the TQEC, said the new site put the university “front and centre” in the city.

“We think it opens up lots of opportunities that we haven’t yet explored,” she said. “One of them will be for students who commute to Bristol, which I think may become an increasingly important trend given that rent is such an expensive cost. Living at home is becoming an increasing option for students.

“It also means that it’s very accessible for a lot of our staff who can commute in, but also for our industrial partners who will be coming to do research and collaboration in the building.”

The site will be a hub for teaching and research across areas including business, innovation, digital engineering, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, advanced telecommunications and quantum technologies.

It features a rare example of a circular lecture theatre. When the Guardian visited, an actor and voice coach from Bristol Old Vic theatre was showing lecturers how to best use the space.

But the university is keen to emphasise that it is is not just for academic types to use, but for all of Bristol’s citizens.

A new entrance from the station to the campus has been created, and new footpaths and cycleways added.

Spaces aimed at citizens include the Bristol Rooms and the Story Exchange on the ground floor, which are designed to bring academics and students together with business, public sector and community organisations.

Sessions on topics important to Bristolians, such as health inequalities, reparative justice and the climate crisis, have already been organised.

Members of the public are to be allowed more casual access to the campus. They will be able to have a coffee on the campus, plug in a laptop and work or use it as a meeting spot.

Squires said: “We wanted to make it a porous place so that people can feel it is a space for them, designed with them in mind. It’s really great to have such an accessible front door to the university where everybody can find it, so we don’t feel so cut off from the city. I think it positions us physically and symbolically in a different way with the city.”

The main building has cost £241m and is named the Sloane Robinson building, after a foundation set up by the former Bristol University student and hedge fund manager Hugh Sloane, which donated £20m.

The West of England Combined Authority (WECA) has invested £35m into the campus and £25m into the station entrance and new paths.

The university has snapped up other parcels of land nearby so it can expand the campus in the coming years, taking the cost of the campus up to £500m.

Behind the Sloane Robinson building, work on the wider Bristol Temple Quarter project is under way in the St Philip’s Marsh area of the city, currently a place of factories, waste disposal sites and Bristol’s fruit market.

Though the new quarter will be 30 years in the making, workers in hi-vis are preparing the way for new homes, shops, community spaces. A bridge is to be built from TQEC to link to it.

Helen Godwin, the mayor of the West of England, said the opening of the campus was a major milestone for Bristol. “Our investment in Bristol Temple Quarter will unlock a giant leap forward for the West of England,” she said.

title: Pupils with Send plans in England likely to double to one in 10 in rush for support
summary:
Schools and councils express financial concerns as EHCP applications surge before potential change in provision

  • ‘Powerful example’: minister looks to Essex school for blueprint to transform Send provision

Schools and councils across England are expecting the proportion of children with special needs plans to double to one in 10, with families rushing to secure support before ministers bring in changes.

Headteachers have reported an “unreal” surge in applications for education, health and care plans (EHCPs) mandating support for needs or disabilities such as speech and learning difficulties, autism or ADHD. In 2025, just one in 20 school-age children had EHCPs.

full_text:
Schools and councils across England are expecting the proportion of children with special needs plans to double to one in 10, with families rushing to secure support before ministers bring in changes.

Headteachers have reported an “unreal” surge in applications for education, health and care plans (EHCPs) mandating support for needs or disabilities such as speech and learning difficulties, autism or ADHD. In 2025, just one in 20 school-age children had EHCPs.

The number of pupils with EHCPs has risen by more than 11% in each of the past two years, and projections by local authorities seen by the Guardian are anticipating similar double-digit annual increases over the next three years. Similar levels nationally would mean just under 10% of all school-age children with an EHCP in 2029.

Such a rapid increase would outstrip the government’s own forecasts and eat into funding for improving specialist support in mainstream schools, undermining its plans for immediate reform while straining school and council budgets.

School leaders said their special educational needs (Send) coordinators had worked through the summer to deal with the influx of requests for assessments, as secondary schools say that many more year 7 pupils are arriving with EHCPs or applications.

One described the volume of requests as “unreal”, while other schools said they expected to have double the number of incoming pupils with EHCPs when the new academic year begins this month.

Bill Revans, the County Councils Network’s spokesperson on special educational needs and disabilities (Send), and the Liberal Democrat leader of Somerset council, said: “It is clear there has been a particularly sharp surge in assessment requests to our member councils this year since the government announced its planned reforms in February.

“Our previous analysis had predicted the number of EHCPs will rise to 840,000 by 2028-29, however, it is now likely these numbers will be exceeded.

“This translates to very real financial pressures on local authorities, and despite the government commitment to wipe 90% of existing Send deficits built up by councils over the past decade, we expect the debt to be re-accrued by as soon as this time next year.”

EHCPs are legal documents agreed between local authorities and families in England detailing the support required for children and young people up to the age of 25, allowing access to extra funding or places in special schools. While more than 530,000 school-age children have EHCPs, an additional 1.3 million have identified special needs, according to official data.

The costs are met out of local authority high needs budgets but the massive growth in EHCPs has led to councils amassing sustained deficits, and require a statutory override granted by central government to avoid many local authorities becoming technically bankrupt.

Georgia Gould, the schools minister overseeing the changes, said the government was carefully considering the responses to its white paper, which aims to give children earlier diagnosis and intervention and moderate the need for EHCPs. The white paper’s timeline would mean more children get individual support plans alongside increased support in mainstream schools; while EHCPs would be designed for those with more profound needs and disabilities from 2030.

During a visit to Thomas Lord Audley secondary school in Colchester, Gould said parts of the planned changes would begin operating this year, including the government’s new “experts in hand” scheme that puts specialists directly into mainstream schools and nurseries.

“I’ve spoken to parents around the country, and lots of families and children have been really let down by the system,” Gould said. “So they are really concerned, and any change can feel worrying for those families.

“That’s why we want to put in place tangible change they can see and feel in classrooms and in their communities. And we’ve been clear that we will build a new and inclusive system before we bring in wider changes.

“We’re really determined to put that support in place so parents don’t need to fight, the support will be readily available at their school, and so no child falls through the cracks.”

Gould acknowledged that it was “going to take time to build that trust, to work with families for them to see that day to day. All the work we are doing, the investment, the teacher training, the sharing of best practice, is so important.”

Paul Whiteman, the general secretary of the National Association of Head Teachers, said the reports of increases in EHCPs chimed with “what we hear from school leaders”.

Whiteman said: “While it is hard to give a definitive reason for why this is happening, it appears likely that the government’s plans to restrict future EHCPs to children with the most complex needs may have led to more families and schools applying before these changes kick-in.”

Ipsea, a charity that helps families navigate the special needs system, said its helplines had received most calls about EHCP provision since March, after the changes were announced.

Madeleine Cassidy, Ipsea’s chief executive, said: “The government’s proposed Send reforms risk making an already fragile system worse by removing the statutory protections and vital safeguards available to children and families when support is delayed, denied or inadequate.”

The surge in applications has led some local authorities to dramatically raise their own forecasts. A report by Hampshire council in July showed applications so far this year were at record levels and forecasted a 58% increase in EHCPs between 2026 and 2030. Manchester council is also anticipating a 40% increase in school-age children with EHCPs by 2029.

William Burns, a social care policy adviser for the Chartered Institute of Public Finance and Accountancy, said a forthcoming survey of local authority treasurers was likely to reveal that the renewed push for EHCPs was creating financial pressures.

Burns said: “The government’s own modelling suggests demand for EHCPs could return to today’s levels by 2035, yet current levels of demand are already placing severe strain on the system. It is therefore difficult to see how recreating today’s volume of need, even within a reformed framework, can be considered a sustainable end state.”

title: ‘Powerful example’: minister looks to Essex school for blueprint to transform Send provision
summary:
Georgia Gould says moving system towards inclusion will mean parents ‘don’t need to fight’ for support in future

  • Pupils with Send plans in England likely to double in rush for support

Georgia Gould is in a race against time. And the minister responsible for overhauling England’s special educational needs provision is hoping that a state school in Colchester will help her beat the clock.

Gould visited Thomas Lord Audley secondary school last week to see the secrets of its success in persuading local parents that it can help children with special needs thrive in a mainstream setting.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Georgia Gould is in a race against time. And the minister responsible for overhauling England’s special educational needs provision is hoping that a state school in Colchester will help her beat the clock.

Gould visited Thomas Lord Audley secondary school last week to see the secrets of its success in persuading local parents that it can help children with special needs thrive in a mainstream setting.

Under the government’s proprosals announced in February, more funding and universal support are to be given to mainstream schools to accommodate children and young people with special educational needs and disabilities (Send).

The schools minister told the Guardian that institutions such as Thomas Lord Audley are doing many things that will become national policy under the new system.

“What they are doing here is a really powerful example of best practice,” Gould said, explaining how the school engages with families and pupils a year or more in advance of entry, and draws up bespoke plans for pupils’ needs similar to the government’s proposed digital records to track and share day-to-day support for children with special needs, called individual support plans.

Gould said: “Part of the work we are trying to do, to transform the system towards inclusion, is to take the best practices from schools like this, and make sure that people can see the evidence and the impact they have on things like attendance … And then we want to spread that practice.

“Of course, schools want to do everything in their power to support children and it’s important that they get a blueprint to be able to do that.”

The hope is that the new tiers of support and national standards will be in place by 2030, when the government wants education, health and care plans (EHCPs) – which many families now use to access support – to be narrowed down to those with the most profound educational needs and disabilities.

But the government’s white paper will allow existing EHCPs to remain in place after 2030. In doing so it may have created a surge of applications from families who fear missing out if they don’t get in before that deadline. That surge means the legacy of EHCPs will absorb funding desperately needed by the new system of support that does not require parents to jump through legal hoops.

“We’re really determined to put that support in place so parents don’t need to fight and battle and go through a bureaucratic process,” Gould said, highlighting evidence she has seen from Rochdale schools that offer early intervention for speech and language difficulties.

“They’ve seen an 85% reduction in referrals for speech and language support because they were able to meet much more of that need at a universal level earlier on, and then those children who did go for an assessment were ones who really needed that specialist extra support. There are models that show this is possible, so we want that early support to be available to everyone.”

Simon Essex, the executive head of Thomas Lord Audley, said the school had earned the trust of parents in Colchester so that it is now oversubscribed.

“We want to serve our community,” he said. “We don’t want any young people who live nearby who can’t come here because we can’t meet their needs.

“That’s our goal, and if that attracts others then we will work hard with the local authority to make it work. That’s why I’m hoping that the funding the government will bring will enable all schools to have the same mindset that we have for these young people.”
